stories.headline: S&P 500 SNAPS LOSING STREAK AS TREASURY MOVES TO CALM BOND MARKET
stories.body: The S&P 500 rose 16.22 points (+0.2%) to close at 7,707.98, its first gain in four sessions, after the Treasury said it will double liquidity-support buybacks of longer-dated debt to at least $4 billion per operation from $2 billion. The move sparked a global bond rally that pulled 30-year yields down roughly 10 bps off multi-decade highs to about 5.18%.
stories.explain: Buybacks work by having the government repurchase older, less-liquid bonds using proceeds from new issuance, which improves secondary-market liquidity and reduces the term premium investors demand for holding long-dated debt. When that premium compresses, yields fall without any change in Fed policy, which is why stocks — priced partly off the long-bond discount rate — rallied even as the Fed signaled it might still need to tighten.

stories.headline: FOMC MINUTES FLAG POSSIBLE TIGHTENING EVEN AS DOLLAR HITS TWO-MONTH LOW
stories.body: Minutes from the Fed's July meeting, released Wednesday, showed 'many participants assessed that policy tightening would likely be necessary' if inflation doesn't retreat — a hawkish surprise given recent soft retail sales and consumer sentiment data. The dollar index (DXY) still slid to 99.46, a two-month low, as traders continue to lean toward a September hold rather than a hike.
stories.explain: The minutes reveal a Fed torn between mandates: inflation readings pushed up by the oil spike argue for higher rates, while weakening consumer spending argues for patience. Markets are treating the soft data as the more decisive signal, which is why the dollar sold off even on hawkish language — investors are betting the Fed talks tough but ultimately holds, keeping real-rate expectations from ratcheting higher.

stories.headline: OIL EXTENDS FOUR-DAY RUN, GOLD PUSHES TOWARD $4,500 ON HORMUZ STANDOFF
stories.body: WTI crude climbed to $86.15/barrel (+1.42%), its fourth straight gain, as the U.S. and Iran showed no sign of resolving the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz. Gold jumped toward $4,518/oz, up roughly 2.9% on the day, as falling yields and safe-haven demand pushed the metal closer to record territory.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of global oil supply, so a credible threat to that chokepoint gets priced immediately into WTI as a geopolitical risk premium rather than a change in current supply. Gold's rally is doing double duty — it benefits from falling real yields, which lower the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset, and from investors hedging the same Middle East tail risk that's driving oil.

stories.headline: CHIP SELLOFF DRAGS NASDAQ-100 DOWN 1.7% EVEN AS BROADER MARKET RALLIES
stories.body: The Nasdaq-100 fell roughly 1.7% to near 29,010 as a semiconductor selloff deepened; the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped to a 2.5-month low with Intel and AMD each down more than 4%. Cyclicals and health care led the broader S&P 500 higher even as tech dragged.
stories.explain: Chip stocks carry outsized sensitivity to rate expectations because so much of their valuation rests on distant future earnings from AI-infrastructure buildout — that makes them the first place investors trim when long yields stay elevated, even on a day yields actually eased. The rotation into cyclicals and health care shows money moving toward sectors priced on near-term earnings rather than a multi-year capex thesis.

stories.headline: BITCOIN JUMPS AS TRUMP PRESSES CONGRESS ON CRYPTO MARKET-STRUCTURE BILL
stories.body: Bitcoin jumped Wednesday as President Trump pushed Congress to pass a long-stalled crypto market-structure bill, with the White House hosting industry executives to build momentum for passage.
stories.explain: The bill would clarify which federal regulator — the SEC or CFTC — oversees most digital assets, a jurisdictional ambiguity that has kept institutional capital on the sidelines for years. Removing that overhang tends to move crypto prices more than a single Fed decision, because it addresses a compliance risk directly rather than a valuation input.

stories.headline: MICHIGAN'S TITLE RUN LEAVES BEHIND A COACHING VACANCY
stories.body: Reigning national champion Michigan enters the off-season needing both a new head coach and a new AD: Dusty May left for the NBA and athletic director Warde Manuel announced he'll step down by year's end. Preseason buzz elsewhere centers on Jeremy Fears Jr., discussed as a threat to the career assists record this winter.

stories.headline: RUSSELL WESTBROOK RETIRES AFTER 18 SEASONS AND NINE ALL-STAR NODS
stories.body: Westbrook announced his retirement on Aug. 12, closing out an 18-year career. Free agency stayed active elsewhere: Bradley Beal signed a two-year deal with the Clippers on Aug. 13, and Cleveland and Charlotte swapped guards, sending Dennis Schröder to the Hornets for Tre Mann.

stories.headline: VON MILLER SIGNS WITH COWBOYS, CHASING A THIRD SUPER BOWL RING
stories.body: The 37-year-old pass rusher joined Dallas as the Cowboys try to get back to championship contention. Elsewhere, Texans WR Jayden Higgins is out for the season with a torn ACL, and the NFL's player-voted Top 100 dropped Ja'Marr Chase and Derrick Henry out of the top 10.

stories.headline: OHIO STATE OPENS FALL CAMP AS THE TITLE FAVORITE
stories.body: With QB Julian Sayin and WR Jeremiah Smith back and new OC Arthur Smith calling plays, the Buckeyes are the betting favorite as camp opens. Defending champion Indiana and a coaching carousel that sent Lane Kiffin to LSU and James Franklin to Virginia Tech reshape a wide-open national race.

deepDive.title: Why an Oil Shock Puts the Fed in a Bind
content: Today's brief has two threads that are actually one story: WTI crude up 1.42% to $86.15 on Strait of Hormuz tensions, and FOMC minutes warning that 'policy tightening would likely be necessary' if inflation doesn't cool. Those aren't a coincidence. Energy is one of the most volatile inputs into headline CPI, and a fourth straight day of oil gains driven by a geopolitical chokepoint threat is exactly the kind of shock that can force a central bank's hand even when the rest of the economy — soft retail sales, weak consumer sentiment — is arguing the opposite direction.

The mechanism runs through two channels. Directly, energy carries a real weight in the CPI basket, so a sustained move in crude shows up in headline inflation within a month or two. Indirectly, and more dangerously, higher fuel costs raise input costs across transportation, manufacturing, and agriculture, feeding into core inflation with a longer lag. This is a supply shock, not a demand shock — the economy isn't overheating, an external constraint just got more expensive. That distinction matters because raising rates does nothing to fix the Strait of Hormuz; it only cools domestic demand elsewhere to offset the imported price pressure, at the cost of growth the Fed would otherwise want to protect.

This is precisely the trap the Fed fell into during the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks, when policymakers underestimated how quickly one-time supply price jumps could get baked into wage demands and inflation expectations, turning a temporary shock into a sustained stagflationary spiral. The lesson central banks took from Volcker's era is that the number that actually matters isn't the spot oil price — it's whether long-run inflation expectations, measured today through instruments like 5-year, 5-year-forward breakevens, start drifting up. A Fed that tightens every time oil moves is overreacting; a Fed that ignores a shock large enough to de-anchor expectations is repeating 1973.

That's the tension sitting underneath today's mixed signals: the Treasury's buyback move pulled 30-year yields down roughly 10 bps and gave equities room to rally, but the Fed's own minutes show officials still nervous that the oil-driven inflation impulse hasn't run its course. Watch two things into the September meeting: whether the Hormuz standoff keeps pushing crude higher, and whether breakeven inflation expectations start moving with it. If they stay anchored, today's hawkish language is likely just cover for staying on hold — soft retail sales, not spot crude, will end up deciding the next Fed move.
